text: Everything so far in this chapter has been about detection and aggregation. This lesson is about the layer underneath that: actually protecting the workload itself. And that layer can't be one uniform product, because a VM, a container, and a serverless function don't share an attack surface.

A VM has a persistent guest OS, so its protection looks like endpoint detection plus vulnerability scanning — Defender for Servers on Azure, GuardDuty's Malware Protection on AWS. A container is built from a layered image you can inspect before it ever runs, so protection splits into a build-time scan and a separate runtime watcher. Serverless has no OS you can reach at all — your real exposure is your own code, its dependencies, and the permissions the function runs with.

On the VM side, Azure bundles this into one plan: Defender for Servers brings Defender for Endpoint onto the machine and layers in vulnerability assessment. AWS assembles the equivalent from separate services — GuardDuty's Malware Protection scans attached EBS volumes, agentlessly, only when it suspects something, while Inspector runs ongoing vulnerability scanning against the instance's installed software.

Containers need two different checks at two different moments. Before deployment, image scanning — Defender for Containers against Azure Container Registry, Inspector against Amazon ECR — catches known-vulnerable packages baked into the image. While it's actually running, a runtime sensor catches what a static scan never could: an unexpected process spawning inside the container, or unusual network activity out of it. A clean scan at build time tells you nothing about that second part.

Serverless flips the whole model, because there's barely any infrastructure left to watch. Defender for App Service covers suspicious requests and connections into App Service and Functions. On AWS, GuardDuty's Lambda Protection watches a function's network activity for connections to known-malicious destinations. But the single highest-leverage control remains one you set yourself: a tightly scoped, least-privilege execution role, since there's no OS layer left to contain a mistake in the code.

Notice the repeating shape across all three: a pre-execution check for known weaknesses, paired with a during-execution watch for anomalous behavior — only the source of that second signal changes. Next lesson pulls everything in this chapter together into an actual daily habit: how to triage the alerts all of this produces without drowning in them.
